summary: Describes the framework for the RFC Series and the RFC Editor function, built on organized community involvement and accountability as the Internet technical community grew. It obsoletes RFC 4844.

plainLanguage.summary: The RFC Series is a long public library of Internet documents. This memo sets out how that library is run: who does the daily editing, who guards the rules, who pays for it, and how four separate groups approve new documents. It is the IAB's statement of the framework, and it replaced an earlier version from 2007.

questions: what does the rfc editor do
subtitle: The IAB's framework for who runs the RFC Series, who approves documents, and how its four streams fit together.

tldr.problem: As the Internet community grew, it was unclear where community involvement ended and RFC Editor control began, and how series-wide issues should be settled fairly across every source of RFCs.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC Editor handles day-to-day operation, the IAB oversees policy and verifies community input, the IETF LLC and IASA fund and contract the work, and four streams each approve their own documents.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8729 replaces RFC 4844 and updates the text for the restructured IASA and the IETF LLC. It was later updated again by RFC 9280 and RFC 9920.

today: RFC 8729 is an Informational IAB document published in February 2020 that obsoletes RFC 4844. It has since been updated by RFC 9280 and RFC 9920, so read those alongside it.

sections.title: Why the Series Needs a Framework
sections.content:
The first Request for Comments was published in April 1969. Since then the RFC Series has been the archival series that documents Internet technical specifications, holding both general contributions from the research and engineering community and standards documents. IETF documents are a large part but not the whole of the series.

The RFC explains why an agreed framework was needed. In the past there was confusion, and sometimes tension, over where to raise issues that belong to one contributing group, such as the IETF, the IAB or independent individuals. It was not always clear where community involvement should end and RFC Editor control should begin. Without a framework, discussions risked becoming polarized: either the IETF dictating the rest of the series, or the series imposing restrictions on the IETF.
sections.plainLanguage: When many different groups share one library, they need clear rules about who decides what. For years it was unclear who should settle disagreements, and arguments could turn into a contest between the biggest group and everyone else. This memo writes the rules down, and the IAB provides them as the body responsible for the RFC Editor.

sections.title: The RFC Series Mission
sections.content:
The mission is stated in a single sentence: the RFC Series is the archival series dedicated to documenting Internet technical specifications, including general contributions from the Internet research and engineering community as well as standards documents.

The RFC adds that RFCs are available free of charge to anyone via the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: The purpose of the series is to keep a permanent, public record of the technical documents that describe the Internet. The second point is just as simple: anyone can read an RFC for free over the Internet.

sections.title: Roles and Responsibilities
sections.content:
The RFC Editor began as one person. The work now needs several experts, and the RFC uses the name to mean that collection of experts and organizations. The RFC Editor is the expert technical and series editor and the implementer of the editorial management of the series, and it is expected to lead discussion of policies for editing, publishing and archiving.

The IAB ensures the mission is fulfilled for the whole community. It has no comprehensive publishing or editorial expertise, so it focuses on principles and on informing and consulting the right bodies. The IAB approves the appointment of the RFC Editor and the general policy the RFC Editor follows.

For operations, the IETF LLC, as part of the IASA, is responsible for administrative and financial matters, and the IASA provides the funding for the RFC Editor. The IETF Executive Director provides contractual and financial oversight and works with the IAB to identify the persons or entities for the RFC Production Center and RFC Publisher roles. The IAB monitors whether the policies work, and in the event of serious non-conformance it may require the Executive Director to vary or renegotiate the arrangements.
sections.plainLanguage: One group does the daily editing and leads discussion of how the library should be run. A second group makes sure the rules are fair and approves the editor and its policy. A third group pays the bills and signs the contracts, and reports show whether the policies actually work.

sections.title: The Four Categories of Activity
sections.content:
The framework supports the operational implementation of the series, based on public process and definition documents, with clear responsibilities and mechanisms for change. It covers four categories: approval of documents; editing, processing and publication; archiving, indexing and accessibility; and series-wide rules and guidelines.

The pattern is the same for each. The RFC Editor handles operations. When a process needs to change, the IAB works with the RFC Editor, the stream bodies and other parties to obtain community input, then verifies that the change accounts for community requirements. Archiving is unusual: there is no applicable process document, and the series continues with the archive built by the RFC Editors since it began. Series-wide rules include the RFC Style Guide (RFC 7322) and the copyright and intellectual property rules (RFC 5378).
sections.plainLanguage: There are four kinds of work in the library, and each follows the same shape. Someone carries it out, and if the rules need to change, the change is discussed openly before it is adopted. For the archive there is no separate rule document: the library simply keeps doing what earlier editors built.

sections.title: The Four RFC Streams
sections.content:
Contributions arrive through streams, each with its own approval process. The RFC says no new streams are expected soon and that it is preferable that new streams not be created. The four are:

  • IETF document stream: working group documents and individual submissions sponsored by an IESG area director. No other stream can approve Standards-Track or BCP RFCs. Its process is the Internet standards process (RFC 2026) and the IESG guidance on sponsoring individual submissions.
  • IAB document stream: the IAB defines its own review and approval process, described in RFC 4845.
  • IRTF document stream: the IRTF is chartered as an activity of the IAB and, with IAB approval, publishes a process for its non-standards-track documents, described in RFC 5743.
  • Independent Submission stream: for documents outside the other streams. Approval generally falls to the RFC Editor, who seeks input from the IESG; the process is defined by several documents including RFC 4846 and RFC 8730.

Each stream also outlines its technical publication requirements. The IAB must agree those requirements are consistent with, and implementable by, the RFC Editor activity, and each stream should deviate only minimally from the shared requirements in RFC 4714.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four doors into the library. Each door has its own guard who decides which documents may come in. Only the IETF door can admit full standards; the other three admit research notes, IAB documents and independent submissions. The keeper of the library must confirm that all four sets of rules can actually be carried out.

sections.title: Security and Changes Since RFC 4844
sections.content:
Publication processes must prevent the introduction of unapproved changes. Because the RFC Editor maintains the index of publications, enough security must be in place to stop outside parties changing published documents. The archive of RFCs, any source documents needed to recreate them, and associated originals such as errata lists and tools must be protected against failure of the storage medium and similar disasters.

Compared with RFC 4844, Sections 3.3, 3.4 and 4 were updated to align with the restructuring of the IASA: under the new structure the IETF LLC performs tasks previously assigned to the IETF Administrative Director and to the Internet Society. Many references were updated, and the wording changed from describing a revised framework to describing the framework.
sections.plainLanguage: The library must be protected so that nobody outside can quietly change a published document, and its copies must survive a failed disk or a disaster. This version mainly updated who is responsible for paying and signing, after the way the IETF organizes its administration changed.
